title: China-Nepal flood is a warning from a warming planet - People's World
description: China-Nepal flood is a warning from a warming planet  People's World
publisher.title: People's World
full_article:
Disaster response personnel carry the body of a flash flood victim for burial at a mass grave in Chitwan, Nepal, Aug. 31, 2026. | Dar Yasin / AP

The speed at which a glacier can become a disaster was revealed high in the Himalayas last week, at an elevation of roughly 5,200 meters (17,000 feet), when a glacier near the China-Nepal border fractured, unleashing a cascade of rock and ice. But what began as an ice avalanche soon became a high-speed debris flow and then turned into a catastrophic mudslide.

By the time it reached Gyirong Port in China’s Xizang autonomous region, it was hurtling at roughly 180 kilometers (112 miles) per hour. The entire sequence from the initial collapse to the devastating arrival of the mudslide at Gyirong Port took only about seven minutes, leaving no time for prewarning and causing heavy casualties on both sides of the border.

Scientists have long warned that glaciers around the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau and the broader Himalayan region—the so-called “Third Pole” and the largest body of ice outside the Arctic and Antarctic—are becoming increasingly unstable as the planet warms.

Glaciers are extraordinarily sensitive to temperature changes, and human-induced warming has been the primary driver of widespread glacial retreat since the 1990s. This continued melting does not merely make glaciers smaller but also destabilizes them, markedly increasing the likelihood of ice, rock, and water moving together. As the climate warms, such glacial chain disasters are becoming more frequent, more widespread, and more destructive.

The glacier was, in this case, more a messenger than a culprit. The years from 2015 through 2025 were the 11 hottest on record. Global greenhouse-gas emissions reached a record high, while glaciers worldwide lost an estimated 408 billion metric tons of mass in 2025 alone—equivalent to filling five Olympic-sized swimming pools every second of the year. The Himalayas are among the regions that suffered the greatest losses.

Yet, when such disasters occur, responsibility is often discussed as though emissions were neatly confined within national borders. They are not.

A smartphone assembled in Asia does not become environmentally benign because its eventual buyer lives in California. National emissions inventories by country generally count pollution where production occurs, even if production serves consumption elsewhere. The result is a peculiar accounting system in which wealthy societies consume carbon-intensive goods while much of the associated pollution appears on somebody else’s ledger.

For instance, while the U.S.’ territorial energy-related carbon dioxide emissions reached roughly 4.9 billion metric tons in 2025, its consumption footprint is significantly higher, revealing the carbon cost of outsourcing production to other countries.

This matters because the climate crisis is fundamentally a question of cumulative emissions. The U.S. alone is responsible for roughly one-fifth of all cumulative carbon dioxide emissions since 1850, with the European Union accounting for about 12%. Taken together, developed nations have emitted 60 to 65% of all greenhouse gases while representing less than 15% of the world’s population.

Rescuers wade through deep mud while carrying out search and rescue operations at the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port in Gyirong County, southwestern China’s Tibet Autonomous Region, on Aug. 29, 2026. | Lhasa Fire and Rescue Mobile Detachment / Xinhua News Agency

The developed economies have benefited enormously from over two centuries of carbon-intensive industrialization. They therefore cannot plausibly present themselves as innocent bystanders when the consequences of their prosperity manifest in poorer and more vulnerable parts of the world.

Nor is climate finance charity. The principle of common but differentiated responsibilities recognizes a basic fact: Countries share a common interest in stabilizing the climate, but they do not share identical histories or capacities.

The Paris Agreement explicitly requires developed countries to provide funds and technological support to developing nations. The pledge made in 2009 to mobilize $100 billion annually by 2020 was met two years late. Even now, the new target of $300 billion per year by 2035 remains a fraction of the $2.4 trillion that United Nations experts estimate developing countries actually need every year.

This makes the upcoming COP31 meeting in Antalya, Turkiye, more than just another diplomatic gathering. It should be a test of whether climate promises can evolve into practical solidarity. The conference is expected to address climate finance, the transition away from fossil fuels, and measures for building climate-resilient societies.

Will wealthy countries provide developing countries the finance and technology needed not merely to reduce emissions but also to survive the consequences of warming that are already unfolding? The old answer—that everyone is responsible, therefore everyone is equally responsible—is morally convenient but scientifically inadequate. A glacier does not know where a factory is registered. Carbon dioxide does not carry a passport.

The mudslide along the China-Nepal border should therefore be seen as a warning from our warming planet. The question at COP31 is whether the world’s wealthiest economies will heed this warning and acknowledge that helping vulnerable countries confront the consequences is not generosity but part of the bill for a crisis from which they have benefited for generations.

हिमालय म॑ जे गति स॑ आपदा बनी सकै छै, ओकरऽ खुलासा पिछला सप्ताह हिमालय म॑ लगभग ५,२०० मीटर (१७,००० फीट) के ऊंचाई प॑ करलऽ गेलऽ छेलै, जब॑ चीन-नेपाल सीमा के पास एगो ग्लेशियर टूटी गेलै, जेकरा स॑ चट्टान आरू बर्फ के झरना निकली गेलै । लेकिन जे बर्फ के हिमस्खलन के रूप में शुरू होलै, वू जल्दी ही तेज गति के मलबा के बहाव बनी गेलै आरू फेरू विनाशकारी कीचड़ में बदली गेलै ।

चीन केरऽ ज़िज़ांग स्वायत्त क्षेत्र केरऽ ग्यिरॉंग बंदरगाह पहुँचै तलक ई लगभग १८० किलोमीटर (११२ मील) प्रति घंटा के रफ्तार स॑ दौड़ी रहलऽ छेलै । शुरुआती पतन स॑ ल॑ क॑ ग्यिरॉंग बंदरगाह प॑ कीचड़ केरऽ विनाशकारी आगमन तक के पूरा क्रम म॑ मात्र लगभग सात मिनट लगलै, जेकरा स॑ पूर्व चेतावनी लेली समय नै बचलै आरू सीमा केरऽ दोनों तरफ भारी जानमाल के नुकसान पहुँचलै ।

वैज्ञानिक सब बहुत दिन स॑ चेतावनी द॑ रहलऽ छै कि किंघाई-तिब्बत पठार आरू व्यापक हिमालयी क्षेत्र के आसपास के ग्लेशियर - तथाकथित “तीसरा ध्रुव” आरू आर्कटिक आरू अंटार्कटिक के बाहर बर्फ केरऽ सबस॑ बड़ऽ निकाय- ग्रह के गर्मी के साथ-साथ तेजी स॑ अस्थिर होय रहलऽ छै ।

ग्लेशियर तापमान परिवर्तन के प्रति असाधारण रूप स॑ संवेदनशील छै, आरू मानव-प्रेरित गर्मी १९९० के दशक स॑ ही व्यापक हिमनदी पीछे हटै के प्राथमिक चालक रहलऽ छै । ई लगातार पिघलला स॑ ग्लेशियर खाली छोटऽ नै होय जाय छै बल्कि ओकरा अस्थिर भी होय जाय छै, जेकरा स॑ बर्फ, चट्टान आरू पानी के एक साथ चलै के संभावना काफी बढ़ी जाय छै । जेना-जेना जलवायु गर्म होय रहलऽ छै, ऐन्हऽ हिमनदी श्रृंखला केरऽ आपदा अधिक बार, अधिक व्यापक आरू अधिक विनाशकारी होय रहलऽ छै ।

ग्लेशियर, एहि मामला में, अपराधी सं बेसी दूत छल. 2015 स॑ 2025 तलक के साल रिकॉर्ड म॑ सबस॑ गरम 11 साल छेलै । वैश्विक ग्रीनहाउस-गैस उत्सर्जन रिकॉर्ड उच्चतम स्तर प॑ पहुँची गेलै, जबकि दुनिया भर म॑ ग्लेशियरऽ के द्रव्यमान म॑ लगभग ४०८ अरब मीट्रिक टन द्रव्यमान के नुकसान केवल २०२५ म॑ ही होय गेलै- जे साल केरऽ हर सेकंड म॑ ओलंपिक आकार के पांच स्विमिंग पूल भरला के बराबर छै । हिमालय ओहि क्षेत्र मे शामिल अछि जाहि मे सबस बेसी नुकसान भेल।

तइयो जखन एहन आपदा अबैत अछि त जिम्मेदारी पर अक्सरहां एहन चर्चा होइत अछि जेना उत्सर्जन राष्ट्रीय सीमाक भीतर सलीका सं सीमित भ गेल हो. ओ सभ नहि छथि।

एशिया म॑ इकट्ठा करलऽ गेलऽ स्मार्टफोन पर्यावरण के दृष्टि स॑ सौम्य नै होय छै, कैन्हेंकि एकरऽ अंतिम खरीदार कैलिफोर्निया म॑ रहै छै । देशक कें अनुसार राष्ट्रीय उत्सर्जन इन्वेंट्री आमतौर पर प्रदूषण कें गिनती करयत छै जत उत्पादन होयत छै, भले ही उत्पादन अन्यत्र खपत कें सेवा करयत छै. एकरऽ परिणाम एगो विचित्र लेखा प्रणाली छै जेकरा म॑ धनी समाज कार्बन-गहन वस्तु के खपत करै छै जबकि एकरा स॑ जुड़लऽ बहुत सारा प्रदूषण ककरो दोसरऽ के लेजर प॑ दिखाई दै छै ।

उदाहरण लेली, जबकि अमेरिका केरऽ क्षेत्रीय ऊर्जा स॑ संबंधित कार्बन डाइऑक्साइड उत्सर्जन २०२५ म॑ लगभग ४.९ अरब मीट्रिक टन तलक पहुँची गेलऽ छै, लेकिन एकरऽ खपत केरऽ पदचिह्न काफी अधिक छै, जेकरा स॑ उत्पादन क॑ अन्य देशऽ क॑ आउटसोर्सिंग करै के कार्बन लागत के खुलासा करलऽ गेलऽ छै ।

ई महत्वपूर्ण छै, कैन्हेंकि जलवायु संकट मौलिक रूप स॑ संचयी उत्सर्जन के सवाल छै । 1850 स॑ अब तलक के सब संचयी कार्बन डाइऑक्साइड उत्सर्जन केरऽ लगभग पांचवा हिस्सा लेली असगरे अमेरिका जिम्मेदार छै, जेकरा म॑ यूरोपीय संघ केरऽ हिस्सा लगभग 12% छै । एकरा मिला क॑ देखलऽ जाय त॑ विकसित राष्ट्रऽ न॑ सब ग्रीनहाउस गैसऽ के ६० स॑ ६५% उत्सर्जन करलकै जबकि दुनिया केरऽ १५% स॑ भी कम आबादी के प्रतिनिधित्व करलकै ।

चीन केरऽ दक्षिण-पश्चिमी तिब्बत स्वायत्त क्षेत्र केरऽ ग्यिरॉंग काउंटी म॑ कीचड़ स॑ प्रभावित ग्यिरॉंग बंदरगाह प॑ 29 अगस्त, 2026 क॑ खोज आरू बचाव अभियान चलाबै के दौरान बचावकर्मी गहरी कीचड़ स॑ गुजरी रहलऽ छै ।| ल्हासा फायर एंड रेस्क्यू मोबाइल टुकड़ी / सिन्हुआ न्यूज एजेंसी

दू शताब्दी स॑ भी अधिक समय स॑ कार्बन-प्रधान औद्योगीकरण स॑ विकसित अर्थव्यवस्था क॑ बहुत फायदा मिललऽ छै । अतः ई सब व्यावहारिक रूप स अपना कए निर्दोष दर्शक क रूप मे नहि प्रस्तुत क सकैत छथि जखन हुनकर समृद्धि क परिणाम दुनिया क गरीब आ बेसी कमजोर हिस्सा मे प्रकट होइत अछि ।

आ ने जलवायु वित्त चैरिटी अछि। साझा लेकिन विभेदित जिम्मेदारी के सिद्धांत एकटा मूलभूत तथ्य के पहचान करै छै: देशऽ के जलवायु क॑ स्थिर करै म॑ साझा हित छै, लेकिन ओकरऽ इतिहास या क्षमता एक जैसनऽ नै छै ।

पेरिस समझौता म॑ स्पष्ट रूप स॑ विकसित देशऽ स॑ विकासशील राष्ट्रऽ क॑ धन आरू तकनीकी सहायता प्रदान करै के कहलऽ गेलऽ छै । 2020 तक सालाना 100 अरब डॉलर जुटाबै के प्रतिज्ञा 2009 मे दू साल देरी स पूरा भेल। अखनी भी 2035 तलक प्रति वर्ष 300 अरब डॉलर केरऽ नया लक्ष्य वू 2.4 खरब डॉलर केरऽ एगो हिस्सा बनलऽ छै जेकरऽ अनुमान संयुक्त राष्ट्र केरऽ विशेषज्ञऽ के अनुमान छै कि विकासशील देशऽ क॑ वास्तव म॑ हर साल जरूरत छै ।

ई स॑ तुर्की केरऽ अंटाल्या म॑ होबै वाला सीओपी३१ केरऽ बैठक खाली एगो आरू कूटनीतिक सभा स॑ अधिक होय गेलऽ छै । ई एकरऽ परीक्षा होना चाहियऽ कि जलवायु वादा व्यावहारिक एकजुटता म॑ विकसित होय सकै छै कि नै । उम्मीद छै कि ई सम्मेलन म॑ जलवायु वित्त, जीवाश्म ईंधन स॑ दूर संक्रमण, आरू जलवायु-लचीली समाज के निर्माण के उपायऽ प॑ ध्यान देलऽ जैतै ।

की धनी देश विकासशील देशक कें ओ वित्त आ तकनीक उपलब्ध करायत जेकर जरूरत छै केवल उत्सर्जन कें कम करय कें लेल नहि बल्कि गर्मी कें परिणाम सं बचय कें लेल जे पहिने सं खुल रहल छै? पुरान उत्तर-जे सब जिम्मेदार अछि, तेँ सब कियो समान रूप सँ जिम्मेदार अछि-नैतिक रूप सँ सुविधाजनक अछि मुदा वैज्ञानिक रूप सँ अपर्याप्त अछि । ग्लेशियर के पता नै छै कि फैक्ट्री कतय पंजीकृत छै। कार्बन डाइऑक्साइड मे पासपोर्ट नहि होइत अछि।

एहि लेल चीन-नेपाल सीमा पर भेल थाल-कादो केँ हमरा लोकनिक वार्मिंग ग्रह सँ चेतावनी बुझबाक चाही। सीओपी31 म॑ सवाल ई छै कि की दुनिया केरऽ सबसें धनी अर्थव्यवस्था ई चेतावनी प॑ ध्यान देतै आरू ई बात क॑ स्वीकार करतै कि कमजोर देशऽ क॑ एकरऽ परिणाम के सामना करै म॑ मदद करना उदारता नै बल्कि एगो ऐसनऽ संकट केरऽ बिल के हिस्सा छै, जेकरा स॑ ओकरा पीढ़ी-दर-पीढ़ी फायदा होय रहलऽ छै ।

A final accounting of lives lost is expected to be in thousands. In the Chitwan district of southern Nepal, some 120 miles from the mountain valleys where the glacial fury first struck, officials have buried nearly 200 unidentified bodies in a forested area because of a lack of morgue space. Mass burials have also started in a forest outside Kathmandu, the capital. DNA samples have been collected so the bodies can be identified later.

Families are still waiting outside hospitals in Kathmandu, the capital, for news of their loved ones. “Even if it’s just their bodies, at least we’d know,” Dil Kumari Masrangi Magar, a woman from Udaypur district in southeastern Nepal, told me outside Kathmandu’s Teaching Hospital. Magar was searching for her missing brother-in-law and a nephew, and had pasted their photos on a hospital wall already covered with images of the dead and names of the missing.

full_article:
On August 26, a glacier collapsed on the Nepal-China border, sending a catastrophic debris flow more than 60 miles downstream along the Trishuli River, wiping out bridges, roads, and settlements across a vast stretch of northern Nepal. Communities were cut off entirely—reachable only by helicopter or on foot. WCK mobilized immediately and teams are now cooking from a community kitchen in the hardest hit area.

Our early focus was Nuwakot Province, where evacuees were being airlifted to a makeshift airfield in Bidur. Families waited at the gates, straining for a familiar face. The moment survivors landed, WCK and our partners were waiting with a hot meal.

Through the first few days of the response, WCK has served thousands of meals—including local staples like samosas and momos.

Today, our teams began operations at our first community kitchen in Gerkhutar, just north of Bidur. Working alongside the Chefs Association of Nepal, we are serving breakfast, lunch, and dinner to families there. Our team overcame significant obstacles to open this kitchen. Road conditions meant traveling just seven miles took over five hours. Thanks to the local knowledge of Nepal Scouts, a national scouting and guiding organization, all the equipment arrived safely.

Two more community kitchens open tomorrow. Community kitchens remain our preferred approach wherever conditions allow. Culturally, people here strongly prefer cooking their own food.

WCK Meal Recipient Locations

As road conditions north of Bidur improve, we are mobilizing more equipment to ensure kitchen teams have everything they need to cook at scale.

The danger to community members is not over. A new barrier lake near the Nepal-China border poses ongoing flood risk, and forecasters are warning of severe flash flooding from local waterways. WCK teams are monitoring conditions closely and will keep serving for as long as communities need us.

Speaking at a press conference in Nepal, an army spokesperson said: “Regarding today’s rescue, since 1700 hours we have rescued 118 Nepalese people.

title: Death toll tops 1,000 after Nepal flooding, as search continues for thousands - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
description: Death toll tops 1,000 after Nepal flooding, as search continues for thousands  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
publisher.title: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
full_article:
LONDON -- More than 1,000 people were confirmed dead and almost 4,000 others were thought to be missing as of Tuesday afternoon in Nepal, where deadly flash flooding last week destroyed towns and swept away structures, according to authorities.

At least 1,003 bodies had been recovered in Nepal as of Tuesday afternoon, the Nepal National Disaster Management Authority said in a post on social media. China's official Xinhua News Agency earlier said at least 16 people were dead.

A total of 3,916 people were said to be missing throughout Nepal, disaster officials said in a 1 p.m. update on Tuesday. Xinhua earlier reported that Chinese officials said some 546 others were missing.

A Buddhist monk looks at photographs of missing and deceased people pasted on wall outside Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, following flash floods and a mudslide, in Kathmandu, Nepal, September 1, 2026. Monika Malla/Reuters

Related Nepal-Tibet flood death toll surpasses 900, officials say, more than 4,400 missing

Nepal's tourism board said that at least 747 people, including some 583 tourists, were thought to be missing in the northern district of Rasuwa, which sits along the border with Tibet, the area where the flooding occurred at about 8:40 a.m. on Wednesday.

This graphic shows destruction along the path of a landslide and subsequent flash flood along the Nepal-Tibet border. Felt Maps/ABC News

The State Department said about 75 Americans are still missing near the Nepal-Tibet border and 14 have made their way to safety as of Tuesday, with no confirmed American deaths.

The flooding inundated areas along the Trishuli River, burying buildings and damaging bridges and roadways.

The wall of ice, water and debris that descended from the mountains on the frontier between Nepal and Tibet caused destruction at least 62 miles downriver into Nepal, an ABC News analysis of verified video and satellite images shows.

Nepal army soldiers work during a search and rescue operation outside a tunnel near the Hydropower Project sites, following deadly flash floods and mudslides, in Rasuwa district, Nepal, in this handout obtained by Reuters on September 1, 2026. Nepal Army via Reuters

Emergency responders were searching tunnels for the missing on Tuesday at Rusawa's Langtang Hydropower Project, along with other hydro-related tunnels. A video released by the Nepali Army showed several emergency responders alternatively crawling and trudging through deep mud within a tunnel.

"During the immediate rescue operation after the flood, 279 people were rescued alive from the hydro areas," the Nepali Army said on Tuesday.

More than 9,200 Army troops were deployed in flood-affected areas, including Rasuwa, Dhading, Chitwan and Nawalparasi East, where, according to the army, they were "coordinating the search and rescue of the injured, assisting in the management of bodies, opening blocked roads and conducting emergency treatment."

A man looks at the "green miracle house" as it stands amid debris after surviving flash floods and a mudslide in Trishuli, Nuwakot district, Nepal, September 1, 2026. Francis Mascarenhas/Reuters

Officials were burying the dead in mass graves, including one in Chitwan, where Police Inspector Anil Thapa said on Monday that 199 of the dead had been buried in one temporary burial area. Thapa said another about 80 people were to be buried on Monday. The national police and the army were helping, along with citizens, Thapa said.

"We found the dead bodies, those are already decomposed, they are already in the state of decomposition, so it was very difficult to put them inside the city area," Thapa said. "That’s why we have to do this."

Security personnel carry body parts of unidentified flood victims, at a mass burial site in Devghat, in Nepal's Chitwan district on August 31, 2026. Prakash Mathema/AFP via Getty Images

The United Nations said on Monday that its officials were "getting a clear picture of what people need." Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson for the U.N.'s secretary-general, said some 65,000 people are in need of emergency water, sanitation or hygiene support.

"More than 22,000 children need protection. 2,600 children under five are expected to need treatment for severe wasting," Dujarric said on Monday. "And around 10,500 pregnant and breastfeeding women need nutrition assistance."

The spokesperson said that preliminary reports indicated that about 107 children may have been separated from their parents or caregivers, adding, "Family tracing and reunification is now an urgent priority."

title: Georgia mom among Americans missing in Nepal following deadly floods - USA Today
description: Georgia mom among Americans missing in Nepal following deadly floods  USA Today
publisher.title: USA Today
full_article:
A glacier collapse and mudslide in the Himalayas caused a catastrophic and cascading flood in Nepal, and thousands of people remain missing as the death toll rises.

More than 2,500 people are unaccounted for, and nearly 800 people have died in Nepal as of Aug. 30. An additional 16 people have died and nearly 550 are missing across the border in China, USA TODAY reported.

Dozens of Americans were reported missing by Nepal's tourism board as part of hundreds of foreign nationals who were in the area at the time of the flood.

Now, the family of one Canton, Georgia woman is holding out hope that she will be found as rescue officials continue to search through debris left by one of the most severe natural disasters in the region.

Cherokee County family waits for answers

In a rescue flyer shared by 11Alive's Kaitlyn Ross, 60-year-old Mary Sorenson was identified as one of the missing Americans in Nepal.

She was in the country for a Mansarovar pilgrimage, a spiritual journey to Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar located in the Tibet Autonomous Region of China. The trip is typically made by those who practice Buddhism, Hinduism, Jainism and Bon, who all hold the location as sacred.

Sorenson was on the trip organized by Isha Sacred Walks and was heading back into Nepal the last time she communicated with her family. Her last known location was at the immigration facility in Gyirong on the Tibet side of the border. She was headed back into Nepal to Kathmandu and eventually Delhi, India to come home. She was last known to be at that location at 9 a.m. local time on Aug. 26.

Videos of the immigration center taken the same morning show devastation as flood waters crashed into building and swept away people and roads.

In an interview with WSB-TV, Sorenson's son said she had texted her family that morning thanking them for the trip and saying she had a great experience.

"She was able to hike up to an incredible mountain with incredible views and swim in an incredible lake and experience all these amazing things that she felt would help her get closer to God and experience God's grace," Riley Wildeman told the outlet. "The group that she was with was able to confirm that she was in the immigration center at the time that everything happened."

According to 11Alive, Sorenson and her husband, Brian, were active in the Canton community, and Brian was known as the retired Captain of the Cherokee County Fire and Emergency Services.

What caused the Nepal flood?

According to the U.S. Geological Survey, what was first thought to be an earthquake was actually the slope failure of a massive glacier in the Himalayan Mountains that created energy equivalent to an M5.2 earthquake. The rumble caused debris and water to flood as far as 62 miles south. A second seismic event was recorded three hours later at a force of an M4.2 earthquake, but officials are still unsure whether the initial slope failure caused the second event as a landslide, or if it was also caused by glacial collapse.

"A glacial collapse is where a portion of a glacier breaks off, and the debris rapidly moves downslope. The glacial debris contained water and ice that rapidly melted, picking up more material and water as it flowed downslope in the existing stream and river channels, creating a fast-moving, far-traveled landslide and flood laden with boulders and other rubble," according to USGS.

title: A week after catastrophic Nepal floods, LI family members get no news about their missing loved - Newsday
description: A week after catastrophic Nepal floods, LI family members get no news about their missing loved  Newsday
publisher.title: Newsday
full_article:
Their loved ones went missing in last week’s catastrophic floods in Nepal, but Aditi Patel, of Old Westbury, and other family members have no new information about them or their whereabouts as of Tuesday.

Patel, 42, believes her mother, Tejal Vyomesh Patel, 64, of New Jersey; her mother-in-law, Amita Amin, 67, of Roslyn Heights; and family friend Jitendra Manubhai Patel, 72, of Merrick, had just passed the border into Tibet last Wednesday when the deadly floods from a glacier collapse inundated the area, she said.

But about one week later, Patel said, no embassy could confirm the time stamp of when the group crossed the border, or even confirm or deny their entry into Tibet.

"We’re not even asking, 'Did you find them?' " Patel said. "We’re just trying to piece together the puzzle."

Patel and Sunny Patel, 38, son of Jitendra Manubhai Patel, previously told Newsday they had spoken with their parents shortly before they attempted to cross the border.

The seven-member tour group arrived in Kathmandu last week and was headed to Tibet to visit Mount Kailash, considered a sacred peak by Hindus, Buddhists and people of other faiths.

The family members said they reached out to numerous embassies including those in Nepal, China and India. But Aditi Patel said it had been a constant "back-and-forth" of going over the same information and no new updates.

She has been in constant communication with the embassy in Beijing, she said. Although their caseworker has been open with the family, Patel said, they also had no news.

"We’re just kind of stuck on this time frame," Patel said. "Both sides don’t have that information."

More than 4,400 people are reported missing since the floods. The Associated Press reported that combined deaths in Nepal and China have surpassed 950. Around 85 Americans are still unaccounted for.

As of Monday, the Nepali government has begun burying victims in mass graves after struggling to keep the bodies refrigerated long enough for relatives to identify them. Authorities say they have collected DNA samples in each case.

As time has gone on, Patel said, she and her family were hanging in and taking things day by day. She credited the support of family members and her community as events, such as her children’s first day of school, passed.

Patel and her husband, Dhruv Amin, both work at a primary healthcare facility with her father-in-law and her mother-in-law, she previously told Newsday.

The couple are considering going to Nepal to find their mothers. But Dipak Lamichhane, owner of tour group operator Nepal Trekking Planner, who is currently in Nepal, is also having no luck in search-and-rescue, both Amin and Patel told Newsday.

Lamichhane’s own son-in-law, who was one of the three Nepali guides with the tour group, also is missing.

Sunny Patel, who visited his mother in Merrick last week after his father went missing in Nepal, said he was still cautiously optimistic for good news, especially after CBS reported on Tuesday one U.S. national was contacted.

"It’s tough, as you can imagine," he said. "We're just holding out some hope that we get some information."

title: Briton among 119 more people rescued in Nepal after flash floods - The Guardian
description: Briton among 119 more people rescued in Nepal after flash floods  The Guardian
publisher.title: The Guardian
full_article:
A British national was among 119 people rescued in Nepal on Tuesday, an official said almost a week after deadly flash floods on the country’s border with Tibet.

An army spokesperson told reporters at a press conference that Tuesday’s rescue efforts had saved 118 Nepali nationals – 44 women and 74 men.

“We have also rescued one British male during this search and rescue operation, and the search and rescue operation is continuing,” he said.

The British man is yet to be identified. The UK Foreign Office was contacted for comment.

The rescues mark a rare breakthrough in a devastating week for Himalayan communities on both sides of the Nepal-Tibet border.

At least 1,050 people have been confirmed dead in Nepal since Wednesday’s flash floods, while Chinese state media said 66 people had been killed in Tibet. More than 4,000 people are still missing.

Nepal’s prime minister, Balendra Shah, said 11,000 people had been rescued across the affected region. This included 330 foreign nationals, the Nepalese tourist board said in an update on Tuesday.

Preliminary analysis of satellite imagery suggests the collapse of a glacier high in the Himalayas was the primary cause of the disaster.

How the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guide Read more

The collapse – so large it was initially recorded as a magnitude-4.4 earthquake – triggered a deadly torrent of water, mud and ice that tore along the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on Wednesday.

Crews have faced dangerous and difficult conditions while searching unstable terrain and flood debris.

Search efforts are now focused on attempts to reach about 600 workers believed to be trapped inside tunnels at several hydropower stations in the region.

“Massive work has been going on in the tunnel, all the tunnels,” the army spokesperson said on Tuesday.

Thirty-six British nationals are missing, the Foreign Office minister, Stewart Wood, told the House of Lords on Tuesday. The figure had previously been put at 33.

A rapid deployment rescue team from the UK arrived in Nepal on Saturday to provide support for Britons and their families as part of the government’s £5m commitment to support relief and recovery efforts.

The Red Cross estimates that 93,000 people have been directly affected by the disaster.

Scientists have said such disasters are more likely as the climate crisis affects mountainous and polar regions.

The UN’s top scientific advisory body said in 2023 that previously ice-bound landmasses – such as permafrost tundra and mountain glaciers – would become increasingly unstable as temperatures rose.

Officials from Nepal, China and Tibet met in May to discuss strengthening their joint response to floods, weather and glacier-related hazards, Reuters reported on Tuesday.

title: Nepal Pays the Price for Climate Change - foreignpolicy.com
description: Nepal Pays the Price for Climate Change  foreignpolicy.com
publisher.title: foreignpolicy.com
full_article:
KATHMANDU—The rains had briefly quelled, and beneath a bright mid-morning sky, 43-year-old Subash Tamang was working along the banks of the monsoon-swollen Trishuli River with his family. They were extracting sand, as they had done before, when the river suddenly rose to consume them.

Some 45 miles north, high in the Himalayas along the Nepal-Tibet border, a large section of a glacier had collapsed, sending a torrent of water, sediments, and boulders and swallowing downstream settlements. It took the flood barely 30 minutes to reach Tamang’s village in Nuwakot district, hitting with the terrible speed of a tsunami.

Tamang survived by holding on to a patch of weed. But it swept away his wife, his two brothers and their wives, and his elder sister. The body of one of his brothers has been retrieved, while the five other family members remain missing. Tamang was ferried to Kathmandu for treatment two days later.

“I’ve lost everything,” he said from a hospital bed. “We didn’t receive any warning and weren’t expecting the water to rise that high. One moment I was hanging by the weeds, and the next moment when I looked, none of my family members were there. I now have a hole in my leg and my heart.”

A crowd of people standing on a muddy slope watching rescuers, with a fallen concrete pole in the midground and a rescue worker in a yellow helmet and bright orange vest in the foreground. Residents survey the damage following flash floods in Trishuli, Nepal, on Aug. 27. Ezra Acayan/Getty Images

The Aug. 26 flood has obliterated parts of three districts—Rasuwa, Dhading, and Nuwakot—in north and central Nepal, but the shock has reverberated throughout the country. The death toll from the flood has climbed to more than 1,000, with nearly 4,000 people still missing, of which nearly 600 are foreign nationals, many of them pilgrims to Tibet’s Mount Kailash, revered by both Hindus and Buddhists.

As quickly as disaster hit, such cataclysmic events have been decades in the making. Carbon emissions have steadily warmed the Himalayas and destabilized its glaciers. A February study shows that the temperatures in Nepal’s glacier collapse area have increased 4.7 degrees Fahrenheit since 1940, twice the average global warming rate.

Low-income countries in the Hindu Kush—which stretches roughly 2,100 miles across eight countries, including Nepal—are paying a grim price for a climate crisis they did little to create. Floods and landslides have become routine and largely normalized despite significant loss of life and economic damage, but a disaster on this scale poses harder questions.

“The ecosystem and landscapes have evolved over geological time, but carbon emissions are changing them so quickly that they’re adapting on a human-dominated time scale,” Simon Cook, a geoscientist and senior lecturer at Scotland’s University of Dundee, told Foreign Policy .

High-angle landscape view showing severe soil erosion, steep mudbanks, and a wide river flowing through a mountain valley near a small settlement. Image 4: Back view of a person carrying a young child on their shoulder while standing in a crowd of people looking at photos posted on a closed shop shutter. Image 5: An elderly woman covered in mud sitting in the metal bucket of an excavator, being assisted by two men, one wearing an orange life jacket and another in a blue uniform. Image 6: A damaged concrete bridge ending abruptly over a wide, muddy riverbed, with a motorcyclist parked near the broken edge and onlookers standing along the sides. Image 7: Close-up of two women crying and embracing each other on a street, with one covering her face with her hand and wearing a black face mask. Image 8: Two people viewed from behind standing on a rocky riverbank, looking out over a wide, turbulent river under a dark sky with sun rays breaking through clouds. An aerial view shows a torrent of muddy water surging past houses and through the Trishuli River in the aftermath of flash floods, near the Nepal-China border in the village of Syabrubesi in Nepal’s Rasuwa district on Aug. 31. Prabin Ranabhat/AFP via Getty Images

Almost a week after the event, scientists, including three Foreign Policy spoke with, have determined what caused the Aug. 26 disaster: a rock-ice avalanche. The glacial collapse and landslide occurred on the northern face of the Langtang Lirung peak—the 99th highest peak in the world—on the Nepali side bordering Tibet at around 8:37 a.m. Satellite images show that a 2,000-foot-wide mass of rock and ice fell from an elevation of 17,000 feet to around 4,000 feet in the valley below.

Basanta Raj Adhikari, director at the Centre for Disaster Studies at Kathmandu’s Institute of Engineering, told Foreign Policy that his estimates show it took about nine minutes for the water and debris from the landslide to reach the Rasuwa border checkpoint, about 12.5 miles from the site of the glacier collapse. That is where waves—potentially as high as 1,500 feet in some places—crashed into the border buildings, hotels, and houses in Gyirong Port on the Chinese side and Rasuwa, crushing people running for their lives—all captured in unsettling CCTV footage.

“The rock is holding the ice, and when it fell both the rock and ice mass broke off, triggering a rock-ice avalanche,” Adhikari said. “Its mass could be over 300 million cubic meters—the size of nearly 120,000 Olympic-sized swimming pools—from our estimate. The energy it created is more than the atom bomb that fell in Hiroshima.”

Balendra Shah takes his oath as prime minister during a swearing-in ceremony in Kathmandu, Nepal, on March 27. Nepal’s New Leaders Go on the Offensive Former officials were arrested over the weekend in connection with a crackdown on protesters last year. South Asia Brief | Michael Kugelman

The thud was so immense that it created a 5.2 magnitude tremor—which the U.S. Geological Survey initially believed to be a 4.4 magnitude earthquake—with the debris blocking the Lhende Khola, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi river, flowing through villages such as Timure and Syabrubesi, before merging into the Trishuli river system. When it burst, an enormous volume of water was released, roaring past the trading posts and villages, which Adhikari said could have been flowing at about 100 miles per hour downstream.

Cook said the potential energy stored in the substantial block of ice gets converted into kinetic energy when it falls, with “all that material being pulverized and broken into smaller pieces of ice slush and water.”

“There were possibly dead and decaying glaciers, too, downstream, which could have been pulverized into the flowing mix of ice, rock, boulders, and so on,” he said. “Some sort of snowmelt or water within the glaciers we didn’t see—it’s common for glaciers to contain pockets of water—could also have resulted in the water flow. Also, the narrow constriction created a funneling effect, resulting in huge waves enveloping buildings.”

An elderly woman covered in mud sitting in the metal bucket of an excavator, being assisted by two men, one wearing an orange life jacket and another in a blue uniform. Rescuers transport a flood survivor in Devghat on Aug. 26. Prakash Mathema/AFP via Getty Images

By the time the ferocious waves reached downstream districts, they had turned into a muddy slush, swallowing person after person and house after house.

Bhakta Bhandari from Devighat in Nuwakot—one of the worst-hit communities—was working on his farm that morning when a neighbor sounded the alarm. He had just started running when the waves violently tossed him into the air before he landed in neck-deep muddy water, injuring his back. I visited him at a Kathmandu hospital, while his wife lay in a bed beside him with severe arm and neck wounds. One of his relatives, he suspects, is missing, with another one dead.

“In all my lifetime, I’ve never seen anything like this,” he told Foreign Policy . “We didn’t even imagine the flood would be this intense. We thought it would be like the previous year. But it was like a tsunami, just like in other countries.”

A damaged concrete bridge ending abruptly over a wide, muddy riverbed, with a motorcyclist parked near the broken edge and onlookers standing along the sides. A local resident rides a motorcycle on the remains of a bridge swept away by floodwaters in the Nuwakot district on Aug. 26. Sunil Pradhan/Anadolu via Getty Images

Studies have shown links between climate change and extreme weather events, with a Carbon Brief analysis from March showing that 71 percent of 504 such episodes globally were “found to be made more likely or more severe by human-caused climate change.”

Nepal has also been at the forefront of such events, with erratic and intense monsoon rains triggering flash floods and landslides almost every year. Last year, an outburst of a supraglacial lake on the Purugu Glacier in Tibet caused widespread devastation in the same area as last week’s disaster. In 2024, the Kathmandu Valley suffered one of the country’s most severe urban floodings ever, and the 2021 flooding of Melamchi River inundated the Melamchi Bazaar.

Other mountain countries are facing similar disasters. From the 2023 glacial lake outburst flood in Sikkim, India, to the 2025 rock-ice avalanche that flattened the Swiss village of Blatten, thousands of people have been killed in such disasters, with economic losses mounting in the billions of dollars just over the past few years.

Miriam Jackson, a research scientist at Norway’s hydrology department who has worked extensively in Nepal and Bhutan, told Foreign Policy that the recent incident in Nepal has similarities to the 2021 Chamoli disaster in India’s Uttarakhand state, where a hanging glacier broke off, releasing energy approximately equal to 15 times the bomb dropped on Hiroshima. She added that the powerful 2015 earthquake also destabilized mountain slopes across Nepal, increasing the risk of landslides and rockfalls.

“Some 25 years ago, you barely heard about glaciers detaching, but there have [been] a few similar incidents in the past two decades,” Jackson said. “Before they were unusual, and now we’re seeing more and more of them—perhaps we’re becoming better at attributing them through satellite images and advanced technology. But these events are huge, and they come suddenly and are hard to predict.”

Back view of a person carrying a young child on their shoulder while standing in a crowd of people looking at photos posted on a closed shop shutter. People view photos of bodies recovered after the floods, displayed outside Maharajgunj Medical Campus in Kathmandu, where unidentified bodies are being taken, on Aug. 29. Ezra Acayan/Getty Images

On the ground, thousands of people are still waiting to hear if their relatives or friends survived.

Outside Kathmandu’s Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, a steady stream of people stops by every day. Their desperate eyes scan the wall where photos of the dead bodies, many of them muddy and naked, are plastered.

Dev Bahadur Rana has been visiting one hospital after another, hoping to trace his nephew, Dil Bahadur Magar, a police officer stationed in Rasuwa. Another man, Risan Tamang, looked away from the photos and called family with no answers. Two of his in-laws, both truck drivers, are missing.

“Once the videos of the floods surfaced, we have been calling, but the phone is now switched off,” Risan said. “We haven’t been able to eat. Their mother and wives have fainted multiple times.”

Close-up of two women crying and embracing each other on a street, with one covering her face with her hand and wearing a black face mask. People cry as they view photos of bodies recovered after the floods, displayed outside a medical campus in Kathmandu on Aug. 29. Ezra Acayan/Getty Images

Nearby, Rabin Lama, who was checking updates on his phone, said that his niece, nephew, and brother-in-law are missing, along with 25 others from his village of Gatlang in Rasuwa.

“I’m sending photos because not everyone can come to Kathmandu, so we want to send them to others with missing family members and relatives for identification,” he said.

A few miles away at the National Trauma Center, people gathered at a temporary information booth set up by the Nepal Police, where Devi Sapkota came looking for his cousin Laxman’s whereabouts. Laxman worked for a Chinese road construction firm on the Syabrubesi-Rasuwagadhi road stretch along the border. The family does not even know the company’s name.

“He had gone on leave three days before the flood and was coming home on Thursday (the day after the disaster),” Sapkota said. “He was going to Timure on Wednesday and taking a bus for Sindhuli. He has been out of contact since then. His wife and 5-year-old son are waiting.”

Families of more than 600 people who are trapped inside the tunnels of as many as 11 hydropower stations are also waiting. They are angry and urging the government to expedite the search for people who may be buried in remote areas near the Chinese border. Nepal Army personnel have been seen navigating waist-deep muddy slush inside the tunnels, while India and Chinese tunnel rescue workers have also joined the search since Saturday. But many are already questioning the government’s initial reluctance to accept foreign help before accepting “specialized” support only on the third day.

Two people viewed from behind standing on a rocky riverbank, looking out over a wide, turbulent river under a dark sky with sun rays breaking through clouds. People view the widened channel of the Trishuli River following flash floods in Devighat on Aug. 29. Ezra Acayan/Getty Images

Nepal ranks sixth globally among countries most affected by climate change, according to development organization Germanwatch’s 2026 Climate Risk Index. As the intensity of such extreme weather events rises, the country is inadequately prepared to face them.

Adhikari, the disaster risk reduction expert, said that Nepal has a disaster strategy, but it’s highly focused on rescue and response, calling for more investment in preparedness and risk assessment, including mapping, monitoring, and early-warning systems.

“There should be risk-sensitive landscape planning that would identify suitable areas for settlements and infrastructure construction, as well as identify risk areas, which Nepal hasn’t done yet,” he said.

Nepal’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, said during a press conference Saturday that the country is “one of the major victims of climate change and its impacts,” despite its negligible contribution to carbon emissions responsible for global warming. Amid growing calls for transboundary collaborations on an early-warning system, he said Nepal and China have been “actively working” to establish such mechanisms.

“Since this disaster, we are in very close coordination, cooperation, and communication with the Chinese authority, and they have been very forthcoming with sharing information and data,” Khanal added.

But climate activists and policy analysts say that narratives around disasters should go beyond devastation to address climate justice.

Sneha Pandey, a climate diplomacy and policy analyst at Climate Analytics, an international climate science and policy institute, told Foreign Policy that the cost incurred by emissions from the richest nations must not overburden poor countries and communities on the front lines. She added that the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage—a global climate finance mechanism—financing “must be scaled up substantially to meet the scale of climate-imposed disasters.”

“At COP31, pressure must be built at the high level to mobilize more finance for loss and damage and adaptation and resilience-building, and to reduce global emissions in line with the Paris Agreement,” Pandey said, referring to the 2026 U.N. Climate Change Conference being held in Turkey later this year. “Nepal must continue to push for dedicated negotiations space for mountain-related concerns so that cryospheric risks are more firmly anchored in the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change process.”

Nepal has fallen, risen, and rebuilt only to be shaken again over the past decades. The end of the decade-long Maoist insurgency in 2006 brought a push for new development, which was shattered by the devastating 2015 earthquake. And as Nepal rebuilt again, the 2025 Gen Z uprising shook the country, leaving behind widespread arson, destruction, and economic losses. But just as a young government took office in March, the floods have now washed away hopes of a fresh start for many. And once again, those with the least are likely to pay the highest price.

Survivors like Bhandari and Subash Tamang, who relied on marginal and climate-sensitive industries like agriculture and sand extraction, respectively, survived the floods, but they feel living with the uncertainty that comes next could be worse.

“We don’t know what sort of help we’ll get from the government, and we don’t know if we are going to be displaced from our home,” Bhandari said. “We’ve lost everything. We only have a pair of clothes now. Everything is gone.”

“After being discharged, I have nowhere else to go,” Tamang added. “I don’t know what to do.”
